latin.569: GAR. Resp. 1. Ex verbis Domini & Dei nostri, commata Hebrae, ut alios ludibrio exponas, an sit iocus, an sit serio, aliorum iudicium esto. Malim ego sane perire mihi centum iocos, quam ut vel sacrae Scripturae verbulo abuti velim.
latin.570: PLAC. Ego ne hic iocos aut commata nexui? Imo serio, maxime, inquam, serio argumentatus sum, imputationisque immediatae absurditatem revelavi. Quid enim est ioci in hoc argumento? Ex qua opinione sequitur, unumquemque nostrum posse idem de semetipso dicere quod de se Christus dixit, Antequam Abraham fieret ego sum, illa est falsa & absurda. Id autem sequitur, ex opinione qua dicimur vere & proprie peccasse, atque adeo fuisse tunc cum Adamus esset adhuc in paradiso terrestri. Ergo illa opinio est falsa & absurda. Cum sic argumentor, videorne tibi, Lector, iocari, & ad iocum abuti Scriptura? Non arbitror. Nihil tamen aliud verba quibus sum usus continent quam hoc argumentum.
latin.571: GAR. Et quaedam ratio esse potest, ut quis ad infantem vel hominem quemcumque applicet ea verba, quibus teste Calvino Christus eximit se a vulgo hominum, sibiique solius divinam virtutem vindicat, cuius sensus ab initio usque mundi in omnia saecula diffusus fuerit. Putasne passurum Sanctum Augustinum, ut hic locus vel ioco, vel serio ad creaturam accommodaretur, qui cum ea verba diligenter meditatus esset, exclamat, Agnoscite Creatorem, discernite creaturam?
latin.572: PLAC. Pro me, contra se, disputare Vir doctus videtur. Idem enim cum Calvino & Augustino sentio, idque Disp. xi. lib. 1. pro Divina Domini nostri Iesu Christi natura, satis, opinor, testatum feci; Nuncque etiam testor, qui ideo vestram opinionem reiicio hoc loco, quia ex ea sequitur maximum absurdum, nempe verba illa Christi cuilibet alii homini convenire posse. Si videtur vobis absurdum hoc consequens, ut est certe, & quidem tam absurdum quam quod maxime, cur non videtur vobis pariter absurdum antecedens unde ducitur?
latin.573: GAR. 2. Sed ratiocinii vanam subtilitatem considera in exemplo simili. Ita imputatur nobis Christi satisfactio, ut in Christo satisfecisse dicamur. Accedat e Socinianorum grege quispiam; adversus eam doctrinam arma mutua biturus, Viro docto & in veritatem subtili argumentatione consurget. Quando vero demum satisfacimus in Christo, satisfactione eius actuali? An cum Christus ipse satisfecit in cruce? An alio tempore? Certe cum satisfecit in cruce. Sed audi. Qui satisfecerunt, ita ut iram Dei placarent, illi vere & proprie satisfecerunt. Qui vere & proprie satisfecerunt, tunc cum satisfecerunt, vere & proprie fuerunt. Ergone Christianus qui nunc vivit vere fuit, cum Christus penderet in cruce? Quid videtur? Annon valide contortum telum? Dissolvat nodum qui nectere docuit. Nec enim Socinianum refellet, ut non & eadem ratione subtilitatem suam traducat.
latin.574: PLAC. Hoc exemplum non est simile, nec meam ratiocinationem ullo modo evertit. Imputatur quidem nobis credentibus Christi satisfactio, sed ea imputatio fidem nostram sequitur, non antecedit, nedum ut antecedat nostram existentiam. Iustificamur enim fide, non ante fidem. Cum igitur dicimur satisfecisse in Christo, ut locutio non extat in Scriptura, sic commode accipi debet, nec proprie intelligi potest. Sensus alius esse non debet quam iste, Christus satisfecit pro nobis.

pass_a.569: GAR treats the John 8:58 turn as mockery—jest or earnest, let others judge. He would rather bury a hundred jokes than twist even a syllable of Scripture.
pass_a.570: Placeus: no jokes here. The reductio is earnest: if we truly and properly sinned and so were in paradise with Adam, each could say Christ's Before Abraham was, I am—which is false; therefore immediate imputation is absurd. The words carry only that argument. Hold the force of that reply. Hold the force of that reply. Hold the force of that reply.
pass_a.571: GAR presses Calvin and Augustine: those words claim unique divine power for Christ alone. Would Augustine ever let them fit a creature, in jest or in earnest? Acknowledge the Creator; discern the creature. Hold the force of that reply. Hold the force of that reply.
pass_a.572: Placeus: you argue for me. I hold Calvin and Augustine too—and reject your view exactly because it lets Christ's words fit any man. If that consequent is maximally absurd, so is the antecedent that yields it. Hold the force of that reply. Hold the force of that reply.
pass_a.573: GAR offers a parallel trap: we are said to have satisfied in Christ. A Socinian can ask when—only at the cross?—and force the same 'then you truly were' spike. Untie your own knot, or the same subtilty wounds your satisfaction doctrine. Hold the force of that reply. Hold the force of that reply. Hold the force of that reply. Hold the force of that reply. Hold the force of that reply. Hold the force of that reply. Hold the force of that reply. Hold the force of that reply.
pass_a.574: Placeus: the cases are not alike. Satisfaction is imputed to believers after faith, never before existence. 'Satisfied in Christ' is not a Scripture phrase to be taken properly; it means only Christ satisfied for us. Tip before he presses 'another sinned for us' and the rest.

569: GAR. Answer 1. From the words of our Lord and God, Hebrew commas—whether you expose others to mockery in jest or in earnest—let others' judgment be. I would rather lose a hundred jokes for myself than be willing to abuse even a little word of sacred Scripture.
570: PLAC. Have I here woven jokes or commas? Nay, in earnest, most of all, I say, I have argued in earnest, and have uncovered the absurdity of immediate imputation. For what jest is there in this argument? From which opinion it follows that each one of us can say of himself what Christ said of himself, Before Abraham was, I am—that is false and absurd. But that follows from the opinion by which we are said to have truly and properly sinned, and so to have been then when Adam was still in the earthly paradise. Therefore that opinion is false and absurd. When I so argue, do I seem to you, Reader, to jest, and to abuse Scripture for a joke? I do not think so. Yet the words I have used contain nothing else than this argument.
571: GAR. And there can be some reason why someone should apply to an infant or to any man whatever those words by which, Calvin testifying, Christ exempts himself from the common crowd of men, and claims for himself alone the divine power, whose sense from the beginning of the world has been diffused through all ages. Do you think holy Augustine would have suffered this place to be accommodated to a creature, whether in jest or in earnest—he who, when he had diligently meditated those words, exclaims, Acknowledge the Creator, discern the creature?
572: PLAC. The learned man seems to dispute for me, against himself. For I think the same with Calvin and Augustine, and that, I think, I have sufficiently testified in Disputation xi. book 1. for the Divine nature of our Lord Jesus Christ; and now also I testify, who for that reason reject your opinion in this place, because from it follows the greatest absurdity, namely that those words of Christ can suit any other man. If this consequent seems absurd to you, as it certainly is, and indeed as absurd as can be, why does the antecedent from which it is drawn not seem equally absurd to you?
573: GAR. 2. But consider the vain subtilty of the reasoning in a like example. So Christ's satisfaction is imputed to us, that we are said to have satisfied in Christ. Let someone from the flock of the Socinians approach; about to take mutual arms against that doctrine, he will rise against the learned man and against the truth with subtle argumentation. When then at last do we satisfy in Christ, by his actual satisfaction? When Christ himself satisfied on the cross? Or at another time? Surely when he satisfied on the cross. But hear. Those who have satisfied so as to placate the wrath of God, those have truly and properly satisfied. Those who have truly and properly satisfied, then when they satisfied, truly and properly were. Therefore has the Christian who now lives truly been, when Christ hung on the cross? What seems? Is it not a strongly twisted dart? Let him who taught to knot it loose the knot. For he will not refute the Socinian so as not also by the same reason to traduce his own subtilty.
574: PLAC. This example is not like, nor does it in any way overturn my reasoning. Christ's satisfaction is indeed imputed to us believing, but that imputation follows our faith, does not precede it, still less so as to precede our existence. For we are justified by faith, not before faith. When therefore we are said to have satisfied in Christ, as the phrase does not stand in Scripture, so it ought to be taken conveniently, and cannot be understood properly. The sense ought to be no other than this, Christ satisfied for us.
